reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A superficial autoimmune blistering disease driven by autoantibodies to desmoglein-1, producing a subcorneal (high epidermal) cleavage plane
Intact bullae are rarely seen; instead there are crusted, scaly erosions on a seborrhoeic distribution (scalp, face, upper trunk)
Mucous membranes are characteristically spared, distinguishing it from pemphigus vulgaris where desmoglein-3 involvement causes mucosal disease
Nikolsky sign is positive, reflecting acantholysis and loss of keratinocyte cohesion in the upper epidermis
Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular ('chicken-wire') IgG and C3 deposition, often most intense in the superficial epidermis
An endemic form (fogo selvagem) occurs in parts of Brazil and is linked to environmental and insect-bite triggers
Drug-induced cases, classically with thiol-containing agents, should be considered and the culprit withdrawn
reference.pathophysiology: Pemphigus foliaceus results from IgG autoantibodies directed against desmoglein-1, a desmosomal cadherin concentrated in the superficial (granular) layer of the epidermis. Antibody binding disrupts desmosomal adhesion between keratinocytes, causing acantholysis and a subcorneal split high in the epidermis. Because desmoglein-1 predominates in the skin rather than mucosa and mucosal desmoglein-3 compensates there, blistering is cutaneous and superficial with mucosal sparing. The fragile superficial roof breaks readily, so patients present with scale-crust and erosions rather than tense blisters. Genetic susceptibility, and in the endemic form environmental exposures, contribute to loss of tolerance.
additionalDifferentials: Impetigo and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Widespread eczema or psoriasis with crusting
additionalInvestigations: Lesional skin biopsy for histology showing subcorneal/superficial acantholysis
Perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence demonstrating intercellular IgG and C3
Indirect immunofluorescence on serum for circulating intercellular antibodies
Serum ELISA for anti-desmoglein-1 (and anti-desmoglein-3 to help distinguish subtype)
Drug history review to identify a possible drug-induced trigger
Baseline investigations before immunosuppression (infection screen, glucose, bone health)
redFlags: Extensive erosions with fluid loss, secondary infection, or sepsis in erythrodermic disease
Rapid progression or failure to respond to first-line therapy
Complications of prolonged systemic corticosteroid or immunosuppressive treatment
New drug exposure temporally linked to disease onset requiring urgent withdrawal
reference.prognosis: Pemphigus foliaceus is generally less severe than pemphigus vulgaris because it is superficial and spares mucosae, and many patients achieve durable remission with corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression or rituximab; relapses and treatment-related morbidity remain important concerns.
pitfalls: Mistaking crusted superficial lesions for seborrhoeic dermatitis or impetigo and delaying diagnosis
Relying on histology alone without direct immunofluorescence to confirm the diagnosis
Overlooking a drug trigger that could resolve with withdrawal
Assuming mucosal involvement excludes pemphigus foliaceus rather than reconsidering pemphigus vulgaris
management: Induce remission with systemic corticosteroids for active or widespread disease
Use rituximab as first-line steroid-sparing therapy to achieve durable remission
Add conventional immunosuppression such as azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil where rituximab is unsuitable
Treat limited disease with potent topical corticosteroids
Review the drug history and withdraw any implicated drug-induced trigger
Provide skin care of crusted erosions and treat secondary bacterial infection with appropriate antibiotics
Monitor with anti-desmoglein-1 antibody titres and screen for immunosuppression-related infection, hyperglycaemia and bone loss
Refer to dermatology for specialist-led immunosuppressive management
